issues.message: Normalized Markdown wrappers, parentheses, compact suffixes or special-case prefixes in 2 mark-code cells before validation.
All mark codes cover the question total, but rows marked as alternative reduce primary coverage to 4 of 8 marks.
Topic/skill classification confidence is below 0.75 and should be reviewed.

skills: Integrate ln(kx) using logarithm splitting and integration by parts or a standard formula
Evaluate a definite integral and simplify to a form a+ln b
methods: Use ln(kx)=ln k+ln x to integrate
Apply the antiderivative for ln x and evaluate bounds

questions.stem_markdown: Find the exact value of $$\int_1^2 \ln 3x \, dx$$. Give your answer in the form $$a + \ln b$$, where $$a$$ and $$b$$ are integers. [4]

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Commence integration by parts and reach $$Ax \ln 3x + \int B dx$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Accept $$Ax \ln 3x - B \int x \times \frac{1}{x} dx$$. Allow unsimplified.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Substitute limits correctly in an expression of the form $$Ax \ln 3x + Bx$$

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: If no working seen, no marks are available.

parts.prompt_markdown: Show that the equation $$\log_4(2x+1)=2\log_4(3x-1)-2$$ can be written as a quadratic equation in x. [3]

skills: Use logarithm identities to rewrite an equation
Convert to polynomial form and solve the resulting quadratic
Check solutions satisfy the log domain
methods: Rewrite powers using log rules
Substitute to obtain a quadratic in x and solve

parts.prompt_markdown: Express $$3\sqrt{2}\sin(x+45^\circ)+\cos x$$ in the form $$R\cos(x-\alpha)$$, where $$R>0$$ and $$0^\circ<\alpha<90^\circ$$. [4]

skills: Rewrite a linear combination of sine and cosine in amplitude-phase form R cos(x-α)
Use the rewritten form to solve a trigonometric equation over a specified interval
methods: Use coefficient matching to find R and α
Reduce to cosine equation and solve using reference angles within the given range

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Using *their* 3 and 4. If using $$\cos\alpha = 4$$ and $$\sin\alpha = 3$$ seen, this scores M0A0.
FT *their* R from **(a)**. Allow $$\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-4}{5}\right)$$ for B1 143.13...

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Carry out a correct method to find a value of $$\theta$$ in the given interval

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Answers may be more accurate for A marks. Accept AWRT 60.0.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Obtain a second answer, e.g. $$84.6^\circ$$ and no other in the interval
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Ignore answers outside the given interval. Accept AWRT 84.6.

assets.description: A coordinate grid showing the graph of $$y = \mathrm{e}^{\sin 2x} \cos 4x$$ on $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \frac14\pi$$, with the maximum point $$M$$ marked on the curve.

relationships: M is the maximum point on the curve.

skills: Interpret a provided graph of the given function to locate its maximum point
Determine the x-coordinate of the maximum point M from the diagram
methods: Use the source-provided graph to read/identify the maximum x-value

questions.stem_markdown: The diagram shows the graph of $$y = \mathrm{e}^{\sin 2x} \cos 4x$$ for $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \frac14\pi$$, and its maximum point $$M$$. Find the x-coordinate of $$M$$. [5]

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Condone sign error. Condone if no attempt at chain rule seen.

parts.prompt_markdown: Find two inequalities in terms of $$z$$ that define the shaded region. [3]
Calculate the least value of $$\arg z$$ for points in this region. [3]

assets.description: An Argand diagram with axes Re and Im, showing a circle and a vertical line boundary. The shaded region is the intersection of the closed disk and the half-plane to the right of the vertical line.

relationships: The shaded region lies inside the circle and to the right of the line Re(z)=2.
The boundaries are included in the shaded region.

skills: Translate circle/line boundaries on an Argand diagram into inequalities in terms of z
Determine the least value of arg z over the shaded region
methods: Convert geometric conditions to inequalities using Re(z) and Im(z)
Use boundary values to minimize the argument

questions.stem_markdown: The shaded region on the Argand diagram shows points representing complex numbers $$z$$ defined by two inequalities. The shaded region is bounded by a circle and a line parallel to the imaginary axis. The boundaries of the region are included in the shaded region.

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown:
Allow $$2 \leqslant \text{Re}(z) \leqslant 3$$
Condone strict inequalities throughout **(a)**. The shading is to the RHS of the diagram.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Obtain answer of the form $$|z - a| \leqslant b$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Accept equation or any inequality sign. Must have $$a$$ complex and $$b$$ real. Condone brackets in place of modulus for this mark.
May be clearly indicated as a point on the diagram. May be $$(2, -\sqrt{3} - 2)$$. May be by attempt to solve $$(x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 2^2$$ with $$x = 2$$.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Carry out a correct method for finding the least value of $$\arg z$$

skills: Solve a quadratic equation with complex coefficients
Express solutions in the form x+iy
methods: Apply the quadratic formula (handling complex arithmetic) and simplify to real and imaginary parts

questions.stem_markdown:
Solve the quadratic equation $$ (2+i)w^2+4w+2-i=0 $$.

Give your answers in the form $$x+iy$$, where $$x$$ and $$y$$ are real. [5]

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Use quadratic formula to solve for $$w$$
Obtain one of the answers $$w = \frac{-4 - 2i}{4 + 2i} \text{ or } w = \frac{-4 + 2i}{4 + 2i}$$
Multiply numerator and denominator by conjugate of their denominator
Use quadratic formula or factorise to solve for $$w$$
Substitute $$w = x + iy$$ and form equations for real and imaginary parts
Form equation in $$x$$ only or $$y$$ only and solve

skills: Differentiate y with respect to t and x with respect to t
Form dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt) and simplify to a rational expression in t
methods: Use parametric differentiation and quotient form for dy/dx

questions.stem_markdown:
The parametric equations of a curve are

$$x=t^2-\ln(2t+1), \quad y=\frac{t}{2t+1}.$$

Obtain a simplified expression for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ in terms of $$t$$. [5]

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Use correct quotient rule or correct product rule

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: OE. Must have 1 in numerator. May have, e.g., $$\frac{1}{(2t+1)(4t^2 + 2t - 2)}$$. ISW.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Use correct quotient rule to differentiate

skills: Separate variables and integrate both sides
Use given initial conditions to determine the constant
Substitute x=√3 and simplify to obtain an exact value of y
methods: Separation of variables
Apply initial values to fix constants and evaluate the resulting logarithmic expression

questions.stem_markdown:
The variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ satisfy the differential equation

$$(x^2+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=kxe^{2y},$$

where $$k$$ is a constant. It is given that $$y=0$$ when $$x=0$$ and that $$y=-\frac12$$ when $$x=1$$.

Solve the differential equation and find the exact value of $$y$$ when $$x=\sqrt{3}$$. [8]

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown:
\int \frac{kx}{x^2+1} dx = \int e^{-2y} dy
Condone missing integral signs or missing $$dx$$, $$dy$$, but not both.
Use $$y=0$$ when $$x=0$$ to evaluate $$c$$ or as limits in a solution containing terms of the form $$e^{-2y}$$ and $$\ln(x^2+1)$$
Use $$y=-\frac{1}{2}$$ when $$x=1$$ to evaluate $$k$$ or as limits in a solution containing terms of the form $$e^{-2y}$$ and $$\ln(x^2+1)$$

parts.prompt_markdown: By sketching a suitable pair of graphs, show that the equation $$\sec 2x=-e^x$$ has only one root in the interval $$0<x<\frac12\pi$$. [2]
Show by calculation that this root lies between 0.9 and 1. [2]
Show that if a sequence of values given by the iterative formula $$x_{n+1}=\frac12\cos^{-1}(-e^{-x_n})$$ converges, then it converges to the root of the equation in part (a). [1]
Use the iterative formula given in part (c) to calculate $$x$$ correct to 3 decimal places. Give the result of each iteration to 5 decimal places. [3]

skills: Argue using graphs that an equation has a unique root in a given interval
Estimate where the root lies numerically using function values/inequalities
Use convergence reasoning to connect a convergent iteration to that root
Perform iterations and present x correct to 3 d.p. with intermediate values
methods: Use sketching of suitable functions to locate and justify uniqueness
Use bracketing by calculation
Apply fixed-point iteration and iterate to required accuracy

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Sketch a relevant graph, e.g. y = sec 2x May be sketching cos2x and -e^{-x} For y = sec 2x correct shape, asymptote in correct position. Cuts at (0, 1) For -e^{x} correct shape, cuts at (0, 1) For y = cos 2x correct shape, correct max/min, cuts axis at π/4 For -e^{-x} correct shape, cuts at (0, -1)
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Complete scale not needed, but should have enough to imply the key points for both graphs.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Sketch a second relevant graph, e.g. y = -e^{x} and justify the given statement
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Needs to mark intersection with a dot, a cross, or say roots at points of intersection, OE.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Calculate the values of a relevant expression or pair of expressions at x = 0.9 and x = 1

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Complete the argument correctly with correct calculated values

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: State the equation $$x = \frac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-e^{-x})$$ and rearrange to obtain $$\sec 2x = -e^x$$ Or rearrange $$\sec 2x = -e^x$$ as $$x = \frac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-e^{-x})$$ and state $$x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-e^{-x_n})$$
Use the iterative process correctly at least once

parts.prompt_markdown: Hence obtain the expansion of $$f(x)$$ in ascending powers of $$x$$, up to and including the term in $$x^2$$. [5]

skills: Decompose a rational function into partial fractions
Expand each partial fraction into a power series around x=0
Combine series terms to obtain coefficients up to x^2
methods: Use partial fraction decomposition with repeated/linear factors
Apply geometric series expansions for 1/(1±x) or similar and collect terms

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Use a correct method for finding a constant
Obtain one of $$A = 1, B = -4, C = 1$$ and $$D = -3$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: SC: If B0 scored due to missing term(s), then a maximum of M1A1 is available for a correct method leading to a correct value.
SC if obtaining $$A = 1$$ and then scoring B0, they can score maximum M1A1 + A1 for a correct value for one other constant.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Use a correct method to find the first two terms in the expansion of $$(3 + x)^{-1}$$, $$(1 + \frac{x}{3})^{-1}$$, $$(2 + x^2)^{-1}$$ or $$(1 + \frac{x^2}{2})^{-1}$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Symbolic binomial coefficients not sufficient for the M1.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Obtain correct unsimplified expansions up to the term in $$x^2$$ of each partial fraction
Multiply $$(Cx + D)$$ by the expansion of $$(1 + \frac{x^2}{2})^{-1}$$ up to the term in $$x^2$$ where $$CD \neq 0$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Expansion of $$(1 + \frac{x^2}{2})^{-1}$$. Must be of the form $$1 + Qx^2$$. Multiplication must include 3 relevant terms.
Or exact equivalent. Do not ISW attempts to multiply expression by, e.g., 108.

parts.prompt_markdown: Find the position vector of the point of intersection of $$m$$ and the line passing through the points $$C$$ and $$D$$. [4]
Find the position vector of the foot of the perpendicular from $$C$$ to $$m$$. [4]

skills: Write a vector equation for a line through two given points
Find the intersection point of two lines using parametric/vector forms
Find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line using projection (orthogonality)
methods: Use direction vectors and parametric line equations
Solve simultaneous vector parameter equations for intersection
Use perpendicular condition (vector dot product equals zero) to locate the projection point

questions.stem_markdown:
With respect to the origin $$O$$, the points $$A$$, $$B$$, $$C$$ and $$D$$ have position vectors given by

$$\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}, \quad \overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \overrightarrow{OD}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-5\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$

The line $$m$$ passes through the points $$A$$ and $$B$$.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Carry out a correct method for finding a vector equation for $m$
Express general point of the second line in component form, i.e. $(1 + 2\mu, -3 - 2\mu, 1 + 3\mu)$

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Equate at least two pairs of corresponding components and solve for $\lambda$ or for $\mu$

Note if $m$ has direction vector $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, then $\lambda = 4$. If line through $CD$ has direction vector $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$, then $\mu = 2$.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Obtain position vector of point of intersection is $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix}$
Find $\vec{CP}$ for a general point $P$ on $m$, e.g. $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 8 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Calculate scalar product of $\vec{CP}$ and a direction vector for $m$ and equate the result to zero
